title: 7.1 Preparing to Track the Campaign
html:
Live Campaign · Pro Analytics · Business application

Preparing to Track the Campaign

Your Brand is the foundation. The Message Matrix turns that foundation into a focused campaign: a defined audience, serialized content and a useful path from each channel back to your website. Before publishing, decide what you want that audience to do and how you will recognize progress.

Pro Analytics brings supported website, email and social reporting into your company workspace on Social Media Magnet Pro. It does not require the old weekly-post plugin or access-token handshake on your customer website. Your website still needs working GA4 tracking; authorizing a connection does not install it.

Start with a Business Question

  • Awareness: Is useful content reaching the audience we intend to serve?
  • Acquisition: Are our spokes bringing relevant visitors into the Brand hub?
  • Retention: Are people returning, and does email give them a useful reason to come back?
  • Action: Are the intended form or phone events occurring, and what do they actually count?

Prepare the Workspace

  1. Open Pro Analytics and confirm the company. Owners working across companies should check the company name before every connection or report.
  2. In Account, save the website, logo, social profiles and intended service area. A saved profile link does not authorize that platform. A location entry records your market; it does not apply a geography filter.
  3. The Owner connects the correct GA4 property, selects Mailchimp or Constant Contact when used, and authorizes the intended Facebook Page and linked professional Instagram account when available. Confirm the displayed account names after saving.
  4. Confirm the event names used for forms and phone actions. Test the intended action with your website/analytics administrator before relying on the totals.
  5. Choose a baseline period and a reporting timezone. Record launch dates and meaningful changes in the publishing calendar.
  6. Invite only the people who need company access. Owners manage connections and team access; Owners and Analysts can request Reviews when enabled. Viewers can read shared results.

The four Brand elements—Story, Promise, Belief and Trust—remain your reference for every decision. A larger audience is useful only when your content and next action strengthen the relationship you are trying to build.

title: 7.2 Platform Insights for Social Acquisition
html:
Live Campaign · Pro Analytics · Business application

Platform Insights for Social Acquisition

Social content is an acquisition spoke. It should connect an audience question to your Brand, then give interested people a useful next step. Start with what the post says and where it leads; use the numbers to understand how that message is traveling.

Read Each Signal for What It Measures

SignalWhat to Look For
Likes and followersAudience size and its reported change. A current total is different from new follows or net growth during a period; use the label shown.
Views or impressionsVisibility and exposure under the platform’s definition. These are not necessarily unique people, and views are not the same as reach.
Reactions, comments, shares and savesAvailable engagement actions. Read the actual responses for meaning; a count alone does not measure positive sentiment.
Website visits and goal eventsWhat happened at the hub when attribution and tracking are available. Social views, website sessions and sales are different measures.

Use the Top Posts as Content Clues

Review the top-five posts shown for the connected Facebook or Instagram account. Check the date, format, topic, hook and destination. Post view counts may be lifetime totals for posts published in the selected period, rather than views earned only during that period. Older posts have had more time to accumulate activity.

A high-view post is a visibility signal worth investigating. A low result is a prompt to inspect content and exposure, not a verdict on the Brand. Compare similar formats and observation time, and use the platform’s native insights for engagement details that Pro Analytics does not supply.

Put It to Work

  1. Choose one stronger and one weaker post aimed at the same audience.
  2. Identify the Message Matrix bucket and the Brand element each post supports.
  3. Check whether the hook, image and linked hub page carry the same idea.
  4. Develop the useful theme, Reframe the weak handoff or Create a missing dimension. Put the next sequence into the publishing calendar.

Direct reporting connections currently cover supported Facebook Page and professional Instagram reporting. Visits from other social sources can still appear in website analytics; that does not mean every social platform is directly connected. This review process focuses on organic content; paid activity should be assessed separately.

title: 7.3 Pro Analytics: Traffic Coming into the Website
html:
Live Campaign · Pro Analytics · Business application

Pro Analytics: Traffic Coming into the Website

Open Pro Analytics → Dashboard → Report. Confirm the company, then choose the dates that answer your question. The Report is a selected-period view of your campaign, rather than the old cumulative weekly grading report.

Select Dates and Compare

  1. Choose 30, 60 or 90 days, one year, or a custom range.
  2. Set Compare with to None, Prior period or Previous year. None shows the selected period without a directional comparison.
  3. Select Apply dates and wait for the report to finish. A changed field is not a completed refresh. Read the visible progress, missing-data or error message before interpreting results.
  4. Confirm the displayed dates, comparison and timezone. Use the same selection when printing or sharing.

Follow the Traffic Back to the Message

SourceInterpretation
Organic SearchVisits attributed to unpaid search results. Inspect the content and customer question behind the visit.
SocialVisits attributed to social channels. Compare the relevant post, link and hub destination.
EmailVisits attributed to an email campaign. Consistent campaign tags help distinguish the return path.
ReferralVisits attributed to links on other websites.
Direct / unattributedThe source is not clear. This can include typed/bookmarked visits and missing referral information; do not assign all Direct traffic to email or Brand awareness.

Use Sources and Timeline to see which channels contribute and when activity changes. A percentage should always be read with its count: growth from two visits to four is 100%, but it is still four visits. Check whether a comparison period had different publishing activity or a seasonal event.

Read the Brand Axis Signals

The dashboard plots session change vertically and change in the returning-to-new-user ratio horizontally. Goal events per 100 sessions are shown separately. These signals help you inspect acquisition and retention balance; they do not directly measure loyalty, sentiment or the reason a person returned. With Compare None, a centered marker does not prove ideal Brand alignment.

Filtering and Missing Data

GA4 automatically excludes known bots, but does not supply the excluded volume. Additional bot screening and service-area filtering are not active in this implementation. Saved service locations do not remove out-of-market visits. Unavailable data is not zero, and geography alone does not identify a bot.

Put It to Work

  1. Save a Report for one meaningful period.
  2. Identify the largest relevant source and one change over time.
  3. Inspect the actual message and destination before changing the campaign.
  4. Use Print / Save for the completed Report; retain the company, report type and timestamp in its filename.

title: 7.4 Pro Analytics and GA4: Behavior Within the Website
html:
Live Campaign · Pro Analytics · Business application

Pro Analytics and GA4: Behavior Within the Website

Getting someone to your website is the handoff, not the finish line. The hub page should continue the promise made in the social post or email and make the next useful action clear.

Keep the Measures Distinct

  • User: a measured visitor identity under the analytics system, not a verified customer.
  • Session: a group of interactions during a visit; one person can have multiple sessions.
  • Page view: a viewing event; repeated views can count again.
  • Entry page: where a session begins, which is different from the most-viewed page overall.
  • New and returning: analytics classifications that depend on available identifiers; a returning visitor is not automatically a loyal customer.

Use Pro Analytics for Direction, GA4 for a Deeper Look

Start with Report → Audience and the website totals. Age appears on the left and gender on the right; geography and device are different groups. Demographic reporting may cover only a subset, be withheld or show Unknown. Do not treat it as a complete profile of your customers.

For page rankings, landing pages, engagement-time metrics and detailed journeys, open the connected property in GA4 and use its available Reports or Explorations. The current native Pro Analytics Report does not yet provide top-page/blog rankings, engagement duration or automatic funnel visualization. Use GA4 for these tasks rather than looking for a missing Pro Analytics control.

Inspect the Actual Hub Page

  • Does the headline answer the question raised by the spoke?
  • Does the content demonstrate the Brand Promise and support Belief and Trust?
  • Is the next action appropriate for a first-time or returning visitor?
  • Does the page work on a phone, and do links and forms function?
  • For the SMM publishing model, blog content uses the /blog/ path. Use that path to isolate blog content in GA4; do not assume every customer platform already follows it.

There is no universal time-on-site target that proves success. A short visit can answer a simple question, while a long visit can reflect useful reading or confusion. A popular homepage is not by itself evidence of a failed acquisition strategy. Compare the intended journey with what the available evidence supports.

Put It to Work

  1. Choose one campaign destination.
  2. Inspect its landing-page and event evidence in GA4 for the same dates as the Pro Analytics Report.
  3. Fix one message-to-action handoff and record the change date.

title: 7.5 GA4 Events and the Goal Funnel
html:
Live Campaign · Pro Analytics · Business application

GA4 Events and the Goal Funnel

A goal funnel describes the useful steps you want someone to take: arrive at relevant content, consider the offer and complete an intended action. GA4 uses event-based measurement. The old Universal Analytics View → Goals → Destination setup no longer applies.

Define the Action Before Counting It

  1. Name the business outcome: an enquiry, appointment request, newsletter signup or another useful next step.
  2. Identify the event that represents it. A phone-link click is not a completed call; a form event is not automatically a qualified lead or sale.
  3. Ask your website/analytics administrator to configure and verify that event in the correct GA4 property. Confirm that it fires for the intended action and does not fire repeatedly merely because a thank-you page is refreshed.
  4. Use GA4 Realtime or DebugView as appropriate to verify collection. Mark an important event as a key event in GA4 when that is the intended reporting definition.
  5. Confirm which form and phone event names Pro Analytics uses. GA4 key-event totals and Pro Analytics’ configured event counts are not automatically the same.

Understand the Pro Analytics Metric

Goal events per 100 sessions = (configured form events + configured phone events) ÷ sessions × 100.

This is an event-frequency measure, not the percentage of people who became customers. One session can contain more than one event, so the value can exceed 100. Keep form and phone definitions consistent between periods and investigate a tracking change before attributing a jump to better messaging.

Illustrative periodSessionsForm + phone eventsEvents / 100 sessions
Previous1,000606.0
Current1,200544.5

Traffic increased 20%, but events per 100 sessions fell from 6.0 to 4.5—a 25% relative decline. That is a reason to inspect the handoff and tracking. It does not prove a broken form or a rejected Brand.

Find Friction in GA4

Use a separately configured GA4 Funnel exploration when you need step-by-step drop-off analysis. Define the steps, sequence and whether the funnel is open or closed before interpreting it. Pro Analytics does not currently build this funnel automatically.

Put It to Work

  1. Choose one acquisition action and one useful return-visit action.
  2. Document the event definition and verification for each.
  3. Check the form, phone link or destination on desktop and mobile.
  4. If results weaken, inspect the content, next action and technical tracking before making a change.

title: 7.6 Email Statistics for Consumer Retention
html:
Live Campaign · Pro Analytics · Business application

Email Statistics for Consumer Retention

Email is the return path in the Social Media Magnet. It should give an audience that already knows you a useful reason to revisit the Brand hub. Keep the 2+2+2 content approach and connect each message to a deliberate content focus and destination.

Connect the Provider You Use

The company Owner selects Mailchimp or Constant Contact in Account and completes the connection shown there. Confirm the provider and audience/account after saving. A disconnected provider or unavailable result is not evidence of zero response.

Read Counts and Rates Together

  • Subscribers: audience size as labeled; distinguish a current total from additions or losses during a period.
  • Sent and delivered: related but different counts. Use the provider’s definition when comparing campaigns.
  • Opens: tracked opening activity, which privacy protections and automated activity can distort. An open does not prove the message was read.
  • Clicks: distinguish total clicks from unique recipients who clicked. Automated link checks can also affect these counts.
  • Rates: retain the denominator shown by the provider. Do not average percentages across campaigns without their underlying counts.

The selected email range identifies campaigns by send date. Their displayed responses may be lifetime-to-date responses for those campaigns. A message sent near the end of the range has had less time to collect activity. Do not describe every displayed open or click as having occurred within the selected date range.

Connect the Email to the Hub

Use consistent campaign tags on email links. Compare attributable Email visits and the intended website action with provider clicks, allowing for differences in tracking and consent. Direct traffic has no clear attribution; do not add it all to Email or describe it as forwarded mail.

Put It to Work

  1. Review the overall totals, then select one stronger and one weaker email with comparable response time.
  2. Inspect the subject, opening hook, content focus and next step.
  3. Choose one change to the message or destination.
  4. Record the send date and review it alongside the same-period website evidence.

title: 7.7 Progress Reports and Pro Analytics Reviews
html:
Live Campaign · Pro Analytics · Business application

Progress Reports and Pro Analytics Reviews

A useful progress report ends in a decision. Pro Analytics gives your company a shared view of results so the team can see what changed, check the content behind it and agree on the next move. Pro Analytics reporting does not grade your company against a class or campaign-population mean.

Report, Review and Account

WorkspacePurpose
ReportSelected-period website, email and supported social results. Change dates and comparisons, inspect the available sections, and print a completed snapshot.
ReviewSaved Pro Analytics Reviews and deliberate requests for a new interpretation of the selected evidence.
AccountCompany details, connections, service-area record, supporting Strategy Canvas/Brand Dyno documents, team access and available billing controls.

Use a Repeatable Business Rhythm

  1. Confirm company, dates, comparison and connection readiness. Wait for the Report to complete.
  2. Read traffic, acquisition/retention balance and goal events together.
  3. Choose two meaningful changes, then inspect the relevant posts, emails and hub pages.
  4. Note a limitation: missing attribution, short observation time, unverified event definition or unavailable provider data.
  5. Write three Moves to Make. Give each an audience, content focus, channel, hub destination, owner, publishing date and success measure.
  6. Return after an appropriate observation period and compare the next matched period. A weekly check can use a seven-day custom range; the platform is not limited to weekly reporting.

Request a Review Deliberately

An Owner or Analyst can request a new Pro Analytics Review when enabled. Use a valid comparison for directional analysis. Changing dates does not automatically create a Review. The company allowance applies to new requested Reviews; opening or printing an existing saved Review does not use another one. Check the allowance and status shown in the workspace.

If you have a Strategy Canvas or Brand Dyno report, an Owner or Analyst can upload it in Account as supporting foundation material before requesting a new Review. Previously saved Reviews retain the evidence used when they were created; uploading a new document does not rewrite them.

Turn the Review into Campaign Work

  • Read the current Brand Axis context and the distinct content signals.
  • Check recommendations against the Brand Story, Promise, Belief and Trust.
  • Use Develop, Reframe and Create to build a dimensional message sequence rather than repeating one generic promotion across all channels.
  • Put the Moves to Make into the Message Matrix and publishing calendar.
  • Use the Report to check the result later. The Review recommends; your team implements and verifies.

Save and Share

Open the intended saved Review before printing. Use the matching Print / Save control on Report or Review and confirm the company, type and timestamp in the filename. Include supporting results when useful. Printing should preserve readable text rather than a giant image of each page.

Put It to Work

  1. Schedule a team checkpoint.
  2. Agree on three Moves to Make.
  3. Assign responsibility and a follow-up date.

Pro Analytics Setup and Quick Start

Use this guide to prepare a company workspace for reporting. Owners manage company connections; team members use the access they have been given. You do not need to create a developer application, set up a separate server or install the old SMM weekly reporting plugin on the customer website.

1. Confirm the Company

Open Pro Analytics. Choose the intended company and check its name and logo. If you manage more than one company, use the company switcher whenever you change clients. Connecting a provider while viewing one company must not be assumed to connect another.

2. Complete Company Details

In Account → Company, save the website, logo, social profile links and intended service area. Saving these details does not authorize an API connection or apply geography filtering. Use full city/state/country information for the market record.

3. Connect Website Analytics

The Owner uses the Google connection control in Account, signs in to a Google account with access to the intended GA4 property and selects that property. Confirm the connected property after returning. If the intended property is missing, obtain access from its administrator rather than selecting another client’s property. Your website administrator must separately verify that GA4 tracking and the relevant events are installed and collecting.

4. Select Email Provider

Choose Mailchimp or Constant Contact if your company uses it. Complete the provider-specific authorization or credential fields shown in Account, select the appropriate audience/account and save. Enter any required credential only in the intended secure settings field. Confirm the displayed connection status; do not repeat a completed setup merely because you have returned to the page.

5. Connect Facebook and Instagram

The Owner authorizes the Facebook account that can manage the intended Page, grants the requested reporting access and selects the correct Page. For Instagram reporting, use the supported professional account linked to that Page and authorize its required reporting permissions. Confirm the actual Page/account names. A social profile URL alone is not a connection, and one successful client connection does not authorize every client.

If a Page or professional Instagram account is unavailable, check the authorizing person’s access, the Page/account linkage and the provider approval message. Some customer connections may require provider approval before they can be used. Do not substitute another company’s account.

6. Invite the Team

Use Account → Users and Invite. Give the recipient the appropriate role and explain what you want them to review. Owners manage the company; Analysts can analyze and request new Reviews when enabled; Viewers can read shared reporting. Analytics-only invitations do not enroll someone in Live Campaign courseware.

7. Verify and Run a Report

  1. Confirm the company and provider identities.
  2. Verify configured form and phone events.
  3. Select a period with known data and choose None, Prior period or Previous year.
  4. Apply dates and wait for the completed report. Read the visible status if a provider is unavailable.
  5. Inspect Report sections, then Print / Save a baseline.
  6. Upload a Strategy Canvas or Brand Dyno document in Account if available before a new Pro Analytics Review.

When Something Is Missing

Check the company, property, date range, provider status and permissions first. Missing history, a new tracking installation or a restricted demographic result is not the same as zero performance. If you need support, share the company name, selected dates and visible error—not a secret, access token or private invitation link.

Social Channels: From Content Signals to Website Visits

The SMM approach is platform-independent. Choose channels because they serve the audience and campaign role, then use the message and hub connection consistently. A profile with a large following is not enough by itself to explain business results.

Two Views of the Same Journey

Use direct Facebook and Instagram reporting for available audience and post signals. Use Report → Sources for visits attributed to social channels at the website. These views answer different questions and should not be added together: a post view is not a website session.

Direct connections for every social platform are not implemented. Website visits from LinkedIn, YouTube or another source can appear through GA4 without a native API connection to that platform. Use each platform’s native analytics for details absent from Pro Analytics.

Inspect the Top Five, Then the Missing Pieces

  • Check post date, format, topic, hook and lifetime-versus-period definition.
  • Identify the Message Matrix bucket and audience question.
  • Read available engagement and comments in the native platform. Views alone do not establish sentiment.
  • Check the profile link, post destination or other supported path to the website.
  • Compare the resulting website source and goal-event evidence without assuming complete attribution.

Put It to Work

  1. Choose a strong content theme and a weak handoff.
  2. Develop the theme into a sequence with distinct channel roles.
  3. Reframe the hook or Create a missing useful hub page.
  4. Schedule and measure the next sequence.

title: 13.1 Email Reporting: Strengthen the Return Path
html:
Live Campaign · Pro Analytics · Business application

Email Reporting: Strengthen the Return Path

Email brings an audience that already knows your Brand back to useful content. The goal is a stronger relationship and an appropriate next action. Use Pro Analytics for the overall view and Mailchimp or Constant Contact for deeper delivery and link details.

Read the Right Totals

MeasureInterpretation
Audience/subscribersA current audience total is different from new subscribers or net growth. Check the displayed definition.
Sent and deliveredSent is not necessarily delivered. Delivery and bounce information helps identify a technical issue before changing the message.
OpensTracked opening activity. Privacy features and automated activity can inflate or alter it; do not equate an open with reading.
ClicksSeparate total actions from unique recipients. Link checks and security scanners can affect results.
Open/click rateRetain the provider denominator. Do not combine rates by simple averaging across different campaign sizes.
Unsubscribes/complaintsRead these with audience fit, frequency and the expectations established at signup.

Make the Dates Honest

The selected range includes campaigns by send date. Reported responses may be lifetime-to-date for those campaigns. Compare campaigns with similar time to respond, audience purpose and delivery conditions. A recent send should not be called a failure because an older send has accumulated more clicks.

Follow the Return to the Hub

Use consistent UTM campaign tags on email links. Compare attributable Email visits with the intended website actions. The provider and GA4 use different systems and will not always match. Direct means that the referral source is unclear; it is not a substitute email total.

Find What Is Connecting

  • Does the subject make a clear, credible promise?
  • Does the opening hook continue that promise?
  • Does the message develop a useful dimension of the Brand, rather than repeat a generic sales claim?
  • Does the linked hub page deliver what the email offered?
  • Is the next action relevant to someone who already knows you?

Make One Measurable Change

Consider seasonality, changes in list composition, deliverability, privacy settings and tracking before explaining a spike or dip. Choose one element to change—a subject, hook, content focus or destination. State what should improve, keep the comparison as consistent as practical, and give it time to respond.

Put It to Work

  1. Inspect one stronger and one weaker email.
  2. Use clicks, relevant website visits and goal events alongside opens.
  3. Reframe the weak connection and schedule a follow-up in the publishing calendar.

Key Terms

14.3 The Brand Axis

As we discussed in the previous section, the infinity loop represents the never-ending process of attracting and potentially repelling customers due to an individual’s or company’s marketing message, i.e., the inertia of the message magnet. As history has demonstrated, some marketing messages are well received and create highly charged magnetic responses. Like a real magnet, this polarized charge would draw in additional target audience consumers along the infinity loop. However, the infinity loop is not uni-directional, meaning it does not always flow unitarily in the same direction. The Social Media Magnet attracts from all paths along the infinity loop, as the consumers can be attracted to the message magnet from any direction. Likewise, a message that would repel consumers due to a poorly targeted message's decreased inertia can also push consumers away in any direction along the infinity loop. Therefore, the infinity loop provides the opportunity to orient multiple dimensions of impact upon the target market. Specifically, The Social Media Magnet theorizes both vertical and horizontal impacts upon the brand. This theoretical mapping of these axes is called the Brand Axis. The Brand Axis measures the loyalty and engagement of a target audience related to their own awareness of the brand in the landscape surrounding that brand.

Within the Brand Axis, the model theorizes the dimensional impact of “Loyalty” as represented by message awareness on the X-axis. Consumers on the far left of the axis have no loyalty due to being completely unaware of the message. In contrast, the consumers on the far right of the axis have no loyalty because they have completely forgotten the message. Note that both axis ends are not an ideal orientation to an individual or company relative to their marketing message. The ideal archetype for the loyalty dimension is directly in the center of the matrix, where the extensions of the infinity loop cross in the middle. However, in the middle ground between both endpoints and the center of the axis, there are varying degrees of awareness that can demarcate skepticism about the consumers’ awareness or forgetfulness of the brand. Consumers who would say, “Yeah, I think I have heard of that brand” or “Yes, I think I remember that brand” would qualify for this middle ground, representing a continuum of awareness on this X-axis.

Along the vertical Y-axis, the model theorizes the dimensional impact of “Engagement” as this consumer engagement is prevented due to extraneous forces on the brand message. At the top of the Y-axis, consumers are distracted from the marketing message due to environmental forces. At the bottom of the Y-axis, consumers are distracted from the marketing message due to competitive forces. Again, both the top and the bottom of the axis are not an ideal orientation on the plot, as the ideal is again directly in the center of the matrix, where the extensions of the infinity loop cross in the middle. Although, again, in the middle ground between both endpoints and the center of the axis, there are varying degrees of impact that these forces may have on the consumers’ level of engagement with the brand. Environmental impacts on consumers might lead them to say, “Yeah, I can’t afford that brand anymore,” or competitive impacts could direct them to express, “No, I like this other brand better.” These types of statements represent the continuum of engagement for the Y-axis.

Now that we have expounded on the nature of each axis let’s look at how they break up the Brand Axis into four quadrants that highlight different segments of consumers.  The four conceptual quadrants are labeled and described below:

Quadrant A: Unaware – Environmental

In this first quadrant, as consumers move further left, away from the Y-axis, they are increasingly unaware that the brand exists.  Those on the far left are completely unaware, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for potentially the smallest of minor details.  In this quadrant, consumers are unaware due to environmental factors that can cloud their awareness.  Those closest to the top of the quadrant on the Y-axis are encountering a large number of distractions due to environmental concerns, while those closest to the X-axis are encountering very few environmental distractions.

Quadrant B: Forgotten – Environmental

In the second quadrant, as consumers move further, right away from Y-axis, they are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Those on the far right have completely forgotten, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for forgetting the smallest of minor details.  In this quadrant, consumers have forgotten about the brand due to environmental factors that have clouded their memory.  Those closest to the top of the quadrant on the Y-axis are encountering a large number of distractions due to environmental concerns, while those closest to the X-axis are encountering very few environmental distractions.

Quadrant C: Forgotten – Competitive

In the third quadrant, as consumers move further, right away from Y-axis, they are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Those on the far right have completely forgotten, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for forgetting the smallest of minor details.  Consumers have forgotten about the brand in this quadrant due to competitive factors that have clouded their memory.  Those closest to the top of the quadrant on the Y-axis are encountering a large number of distractions due to competitive factors, while those closest to the X-axis are encountering very few competitive distractions.

 Quadrant D: Unaware – Competitive

In the fourth and last quadrant, as consumers move further left, away from the Y-axis, they are increasingly unaware that the brand exists.  Those on the far left are completely unaware, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for potentially the smallest of minor details.  In this quadrant, consumers are unaware due to competitive factors that can cloud their awareness.  Those closest to the top of the quadrant on the Y-axis are encountering a large number of distractions due to competitive concerns, while those closest to the X-axis are encountering very few competitive distractions.

14.4 The Strategic Impact of the Brand Axis

In The Social Media Magnet Theory, the perfect strategic brand alignment, called magnetic alignment, of the message magnet is centered over the intersection of the Loyalty (X-axis) and Engagement (Y-axis) on the Brand Axis.  At this point, the company’s (or individual’s) message magnet is also centered in the infinity loop, demonstrating that the brand elements align with the target market's desired perceptions.  The perfect alignment of the message magnet on the brand axis would like this:

In this perfect magnetic alignment, the target market consumers within the message magnet's boundaries (i.e., within the blue border of the message magnet above) are not part of the Brand Axis quadrants.  Because they are continually within reach of the brand’s targeted marketing messages, even though they may be on the edge of the boundary, there are no environmental or competitive forces acting strong enough on them to have them unaware or have forgotten about the brand.  In this ideal scenario, the message magnet is permanently centered right in the middle of the infinity loop. The loop is directly aligned at the center with the engagement and loyalty axes. Here, the marketing message is completely on-brand, and consumers on the infinity loop within the boundaries of the message magnet are the ideal target audience.  The message magnet will actually grow in size as the company (or individual) maintains this balance and grows its reach.  For example, as discussed in Chapter 2, Coke’s message magnet would nearly envelop the whole infinity loop as few consumers are unaware or have forgotten about Coca-Cola as a soft-drink choice. In contrast, new startup companies would have a very small message magnet on the Brand Axis.

Therefore, as these examples demonstrate, the Brand Axis acts as a map and compass for any company (or individual) running an inbound marketing campaign. Although while it would be ideal to have the message magnet centered on the Brand Axis permanently, numerous consulting opportunities in this domain have demonstrated to the author’s that it does not take long for the message magnet to become misaligned, or in other words, the message magnet can drift off the center of the loyalty and engagement axes. This event, called magnetic misalignment, can occur due to internal decisions (made within a company or by an individual) or external factors (occurrences out of the control of a company or an individual) that cause the message magnet to move off-center of the Brand Axis.  At times this might indicate that a company’s (or individual’s) marketing message is not being denoted correctly by the target audience or that the company’s marketing message is becoming off-target.  In this scenario, whether it is competitive or environmental factors contributing to this misalignment, it can happen quickly and is often hard to identify. For example, examine the following hypothetical scenario with the Brand Axis.

In this example, the message matrix has drifted directly left of the engagement axis into a neither environmentally nor competitively restrictive landscape. Therefore, this company’s messaging has attracted consumers who have never heard of the brand before. This is an acquisition strategy that has become misaligned, as the company is over-focused on new clients. This happens very frequently with some companies as they worry about growth. We would contend that at the same time, they are hypervigilant in attracting new customers. There are very loyal customers seeping out the back door of their strategy due to messaging efforts that do not speak to these loyal customers. For example, take a pop-up advertisement on a website that provides a 20% coupon off of a customer’s first order. While this may be appealing to signing up new customers for the first time, what does this indicate to loyal customers who purchase from the site often? Where is their 20% coupon, have they not earned it? Now, this is not to say that new acquisition strategies are not important. It just shouldn’t utilize the messaging space on the front of the website where loyal customers are certain to be perusing the site.

As you can see in this example, the brand axis is a monitoring tool for companies (and individuals) running social media campaigns regarding their message orientation. These authors contend that if and when a message magnet is determined to be misaligned, it should return to its key brand elements to re-center the message magnet.  We will explore these ideas further in the final chapter as we focus on the question: What happens when an individual or company’s message becomes misaligned?

title: 15.1 Strategic Misalignments in Each Brand Axis Quadrant
html:
15.1 Strategic Misalignments in Each Brand Axis Quadrant

What happens when an individual or company’s message becomes misaligned, or in other words, off-brand?  While a magnetic misalignment causes the message magnet to move away from being centered on the Brand Axis, this conceptually implies the individual’s or company’s message no longer supports the brand hub strategy or the four brand elements.

  • Misaligned push scenarios are due to a company’s own internal strategic decisions. In these “push” cases, a hyper-focus on a quadrant of consumers can cause a company to become misaligned, moving the message magnet from the center of the Brand Axis into the focused quadrant.
  • Misaligned pull scenarios are due to external forces acting on a company or individual, causing them to move off-center of the Brand Axis.

Many times, especially in small to medium-sized businesses, owners seemingly chase an opportunity that will create new marketing messages that are incongruent with the main message of the firm. In these instances, these owners need to return to the primary message. They need to remember to: "Keep the main thing the main thing.” For example, if you are a physical therapy clinic, you shouldn’t run messaging that you do hearing tests. While physical therapy may often assist people with vertigo because they have inner-ear problems, balance disorder is the main thing. Yes, there is a connection between hearing and inner-ear issues. While you may holistically want to help these patients with inner-ear disorders, the clinic needs to remember that it does not specialize in audiology but physical therapy. It is these authors’ experience that this is a frequent occurrence in the marketplace. Furthermore, when the messaging becomes off-brand, current conversions that help maintain the business’s normal operating efficiencies will be disrupted.

It is imperative here to stress the critical importance of keeping The Social Media Magnet adequately balanced. This requires messages to remain centered on the four brand elements discussed in Chapter 2. Successful inbound marketing campaigns reinforce the brand story, promise, and beliefs while maintaining and building levels of trust with consumers. If the message wanders off-brand, unforeseen consequences mentioned above can occur, like focusing on the wrong target market or presenting marketing messages that do not resonate with the target audience. Furthermore, these effects could result from poor internal managerial decisions or from outside the firm in the form of environmental or competitive forces changing consumer perceptions. A managerial perspective focused on the core brand elements will bring the Social Media Magnet back into alignment and stabilize the social model in any of these situations.

Recall that the Brand Axis is divided into four quadrants as partitioned by the Loyalty and Engagement axes.  Left of the Engagement axis are consumers who register as unaware on the loyalty scale. For these consumers who are unaware, the Brand Axis indicates those consumers are unaware either due to the environmental landscape forces or competitive landscape forces. In the top left quadrant, the matrix represents consumers who have not heard the company’s (or individual’s) marketing message due to the environmental landscape. Whether socio-economic, cultural, regulatory forces, etc., these consumers are unaware of the brand messaging. However, in the bottom left quadrant, the matrix represents consumers who have not heard the company's (or individual’s) marketing message due to the competitive landscape. In these instances, competitors have inhibited the targeted audience from hearing the brand message. For example, it could be that the competition has a larger overall marketing budget, and the sheer volume of their messages is drowning out the company’s (or individual’s) attempt to communicate.

 

However, consumers mapped to the right of the Engagement axis are not loyal to the brand because they have forgotten about the brand. These are consumers who were aware of the brand and message, but over time have moved away as the brand fell from their consideration set. For these consumers that have forgotten the brand, the Brand Axis also identifies their extinction based on either environmental or competitive landscape forces. In the top-right quadrant, the matrix represents consumers who have forgotten about the company’s (or individual’s) marketing message due to the environmental landscape. Whether socio-economic, cultural, regulatory forces, etc., these consumers who were once in tune with the brand have moved away from the brand messaging. However, in the bottom right quadrant, the matrix represents consumers who have forgotten about the company’s (or individual’s) marketing message due to the competitive landscape. In these instances, competitors have inhibited the targeted audience from remembering the brand message. For example, it could be that the competition has a more valuable offering. The consumer has forgotten about the company’s (or individual’s) product completely, or to some degree relative to the competitor’s product offerings.

In the following sections, we will deeply explore each of the Brand Axis Quadrants, focusing on potential internal decisions and external factors that could pull or push the message magnet off the center of the Brand Axis and towards a specific quadrant.  Finally, we will end each section with potential remedies on how to re-align the message magnet to the center of the Brand Axis.

title: 15.2 Quadrant A: Acquisition Focus within Environmental Uncertainty

15.2 Quadrant A: Acquisition Focus within Environmental Uncertainty

The first quadrant of the Brand Axis includes consumers who are typically unaware of the company’s (or individual’s) brand due to environmental distractions.  As discussed in the previous chapters, consumers closest to the X-axis are conceptually less distracted by uncertain environmental conditions, while those further away from the same axis are more distracted by uncertain environmental conditions.  Likewise, consumers closest to the Y-axis are conceptually more aware than those further away from the same axis.

The Situation

When companies (or individuals) begin to target consumers in this quadrant, they have become magnetically misaligned as an acquisition strategy to focus more heavily on ascertaining new customers that never have, or very rarely, purchased their product or service previously.  However, in this particular quadrant, these consumers are not distracted by competitive offerings but are uncertain of the product due to environmental constraints.  These environmental constraints can include socio-economic, political/regulatory, cultural, or technological forces that prohibit consumers from purchasing.  Whether the reason includes not having enough money, not having the technological ability, not having a cultural significance, or not having access to the product or service, consumers in this quadrant do not know that the product or service is even available.  This lack of awareness keeps them outside of the targeted audience of the balanced message magnet centered over the direct middle of the Brand Axis.

When conducting a situational analysis, companies (or individuals) may become aware and too focused on accessing these consumers at the expense of their entire branding message.  This is known as a misaligned push scenario, which is due to a company’s (or individual’s) own internal strategic decisions.  In these “push” cases, a hyper-focus on a quadrant of consumers can cause a company to become misaligned, moving the message magnet from the center of the Brand Axis into the focused quadrant.  [Note, a market share growth into this quadrant is possible with a balanced message over time, meaning that the size of the message magnet can grow and expand further into this quadrant, but a misaligned move into this quadrant often comes in haste, trying to capture these potential customers without a balanced campaign.]  A rush to capture more consumers in the quadrant causes the message magnet to become off-brand, causing the current message magnet not to grow but to move off-center.  As it moves into this quadrant, less of the message magnet becomes equally shared by the other three quadrants.

For example, in the scenario above, you can see that the internal decisions of this firm have pushed the message magnet off-center.  The push structure is indicated by the hub, which is typically in the center of the message magnet where the brand and the brand spokes consist, which has moved closer to the edge of the message magnet border, insinuating that it is pushing the entire message magnet off-center. This means that this misaligned push approach has increased Quadrant A from a balanced approach of 25% to an unbalanced level of 70% of the marketing message. In this case, the other quadrants, which when balanced would all be equal to 25% of the message, have become disproportionate, decreasing to 12%, 4%, and 14%, respectively across the other quadrants.

The previous discussion focused on the internal decisions that cause companies (or individuals) to push the message magnet into misalignment inadvertently.  In another realistic scenario, companies can also be pulled by environmental factors into the same position.  As you can see in the example above, the percentages of targeted customers from each quadrant stay the same. Still, the hub has moved into the bottom right of the message magnet, demonstrating that it is being pulled in the direction of Quadrant A.  This is known as a misaligned pull scenario, which is due to external forces acting on a company or individual, causing them to move off the center of the Brand Axis.  Here, the hub of the magnet is trying to stay on center due to marketing messages that attempt to stay on brand; however, external forces are naturally pulling the company or individual message in that direction away from the centered position on the brand axis.

In this quadrant, these external forces can be the same environmental forces that are making consumers unaware that the brand exists, and even though the company may not internally decide to change its messaging to address this environmental uncertainty to acquire new customers, there in some cases may be no way to avoid it.   This is not atypical of regulatory and technological changes in the environment.  When major laws are passed, like the Patriot Act, some industries are pulled into a particular stance with their messaging.  While they may not want to address or discuss these issues within their marketing space to gain new customers, they may have no choice but to address these new policy issues, which could naturally pull them off the center of the Brand Axis.  While this external scenario may not be as prevalent as the internal one in this quadrant, it can happen in certain industries.

The Impacts

As highlighted in the percentage numbers in the graphics above, the impact of this quadrant becomes overly focused on new customers.  While a company either intentionally (internal push misalignment) or unintentionally (external pull misalignment) moves into this quadrant due to environmental uncertainty, loyal customers are slipping out the back door.  This misalignment creates major inefficiencies due to the decreased impact of returning customers.  As you can tell from the percentages below, only 16% of the marketing message is now organically directed at returning customers, which is a decrease of 34%.  Hypothetically speaking, if a company or individual were to lose 34% of the existing or returning revenue, there most likely would be an immense amount of revenue loss.  However, this scenario occurs every day as firms become overly aggressive to move into new markets.  It can sometimes occur even when trying to stay balanced but are pulled into this quadrant due to changing environmental conditions.

15.3 Quadrant B: Retention Focus within Environmental Uncertainty

The second quadrant of the Brand Axis includes consumers who have typically forgotten about the company’s (or individual’s) brand due to environmental distractions.  As discussed in the previous chapters, consumers closest to the X-axis are conceptually less distracted by uncertain environmental conditions, while those further away from the same axis are more distracted by uncertain environmental conditions.  Likewise, consumers further away from Y-axis are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Those on the far right have completely forgotten, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for forgetting the smallest of minor details.

The Situation

When companies (or individuals) begin to target consumers in this quadrant, they have become magnetically misaligned as a retention strategy to focus more heavily on retaining loyal customers that have frequently purchased their product or service previously but are beginning to forget about the product or service.  However, in this particular quadrant, these consumers are not distracted by competitive offerings but are uncertain of the product due to environmental constraints.  As previously discussed, these environmental constraints can include socio-economic, political/regulatory, cultural, or technological forces that prohibit a consumer from repurchasing.  Whether the reason includes a reduction in income, cultural relevance, technological know-how, or the recent inability to access the product or service, consumers in this quadrant are moving away from purchasing this brand, even though they may have purchased in the past.  This extinction of the brand in the consumer's mind has made them no longer a target audience of the balanced message magnet but into space beyond the magnet’s border.

When conducting a situational analysis, companies (or individuals) may become aware of their previous consumers’ movement away from the brand and become overly focused on retaining these customers at the expense of their entire branding message.  Again, this misaligned push scenario results from an internal decision to recapture these consumers while reducing the balanced attention on acquiring new customers at the same time. As discussed in previous sections, Quadrant C is similar in that a firm can be “pulled” into magnetic misalignment.  In this quadrant, the same competitive forces that make consumers forget that the brand exists are causing the brand to become misaligned.  Even though the company may not internally decide to change its messaging to address these exact competitors’ attempts to steal market share, competitive advertising may thrust the company (or individual) into the heat of the battle.  In fact, for this very reason, some countries do not allow competitive advertising.  Like in South Africa, the practice is considered illegal, although, in the United States, we see it all of the time (e.g., Ford vs. Chevy Trucks).  In this example, some companies (or individuals) can be pulled into misalignment by the actions of competing firms, which could naturally pull them off the center of the Brand Axis, as indicated in the figure below.

15.5 Quadrant D: Acquisition Focus within Competitive Intensity

The fourth and final quadrant consumers are typically unaware of the company’s (or individual’s) brand due to competitive intensity.  As discussed in the previous chapters, consumers positioned closest to the X-axis are conceptually less distracted by competitive messages, while those further away from the same axis are more distracted by competitors.  Likewise, consumers further away from Y-axis are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Likewise, consumers closest to the Y-axis are conceptually more aware of the brand than those further away from the same axis.

The Situation

When companies (or individuals) begin to target consumers in this quadrant, they have become magnetically misaligned as an acquisition strategy to focus more heavily on establishing new customers.  These consumers have never, or very rarely, purchased the brand previously due to having already been persuaded by other competing brands.  For many possible different reasons, these competitors have already gained the appeal of the target consumers before the customer might even consider the company’s (or individual’s) brand.  In most instances, the value equation of the competing brand has already convinced consumers towards their brand due to a competitive advantage across one or more of the four P’s: Product, Place, Price, or Promotion.  The unawareness of the company’s (or individual’s) brand in the consumer's mind has prevented them from entering into the borders of a balanced message magnet, as the consumer has never previously become part of the company’s (or individual’s) target market.

When conducting a situational analysis, companies (or individuals) may become aware and too focused on accessing these consumers at the expense of their entire branding message.  Again, this misaligned push scenario results from an internal decision to capture these consumers while reducing the balanced attention on retaining new customers at the same time.  As demonstrated in the example below, the message magnet becomes unbalanced, causing the company to move 70% of its messaging focus into this quadrant and away from the other three quadrants.  As you can see, the internal decisions of this firm have pushed the message magnet off-center.  In this case, the other quadrants have decreased to 12%, 4%, and 14%, respectively, across the other quadrants.  This means that this misaligned push approach in Quadrant D has increased from a balanced 25% to an unbalanced level of 70% of the marketing message.

As discussed in previous sections, Quadrant D is similar in that a firm can also experience a misaligned pull scenario.  In this quadrant, the same competitive forces that are making consumers unaware that the company’s (or individual’s) brand exists are causing the brand to become misaligned.  Even though the company may not internally decide to change its messaging to address these exact competitors’ attempt to allow any consideration of another brand, the saturation of a competitor’s message within the overall market may demand that the company (or individual) address their own competitive disadvantages in the marketplace. In this example, the company (or individual) can be pulled into misalignment by the mere marketing actions of competing firms, which would force them to move towards consumers that may have never heard of their brand, or at least, very little about the brand.  In this example, the sheer lack of market share due to the competitive dominance of other brands can move the message magnet off-center of the Brand Axis, as indicated in the figure below.

The Impacts

As highlighted in the percentage numbers in the graphics above, the impact of this quadrant becomes overly focused on acquiring new customers at the expense of retaining previous ones.  While a company either intentionally (internal push misalignment) or unintentionally (external pull misalignment) moves into this quadrant due to competitive intensity, opportunities in keeping prior customers are being overlooked.  Just like in Quadrant A, this misalignment creates inefficiencies due to the decreased impact of previous customers.  As demonstrated from the percentages above, only 16% of the marketing message is now organically directed at loyal customers, a decrease of 34%.  Hypothetically speaking, if a company or individual were to lose 34% of potential new revenue, there most likely would be an immense amount of profit loss because the same return is unlikely in acquiring new customers who have never heard of the brand due to competitive intensity.  As with all other quadrants, the misalignment creates unequaled opportunity, resulting in fewer sales and lost profit.  Although this scenario occurs every day as firms become overly aggressive to acquire new customers at the expense of their competitors, they are just being pulled into this quadrant due to competition intensity.

title: 15.6 The Remedy to Magnetic Misalignment
html:
15.6 The Remedy to Magnetic Misalignment

Whether it is a misaligned push or pull scenario, companies (or individuals) that find themselves in any of these quadrants need to return to their four brand elements with a strategic intent to stay balanced between new and returning customers.  When considering the four brand elements, companies (or individuals) need to consider the following: the brand story, their brand promises, their brand beliefs, and brand trust. To bring the message magnet back into alignment, the brand must return to its original story to refocus the brand messages.

Much like a mission statement, the brand story requires that every other brand decision and brand message must build upon the story. In any future decision, if the outcome is in opposition to the brand story, then one should decide against it.  The story is about the personal journey that the company or individual has taken in creating the brand.  It can be about how the company (or individual) came up with the idea, product, or service. Or it could be metaphoric, and while it may not be an actual story, it would be a realistic narrative around the concept or idea. The story answers questions about the emotion, authenticity, and historical nature of the brand.  It helps identify who would want or need the brand and how it fulfills those desires.  The story lays the foundation for the brand promises that the individual or company will always uphold.

If the brand story is a mission statement, then the brand promise is the vision statement. What are those things that a company will promise to do for its customers, and how do they intend to keep this promise?  Brand promises give way to brand beliefs, which are the pillars of value that a company believes about the brand and attempts to convince their consumers to believe about the brand.  These values are built upon the foundation of the brand story and the brand promises, all combining together to invoke brand trust.  Brand trust is a personal relationship built over time as satisfaction by both parties, brand and consumer alike, is accomplished and repeated repeatedly.

A Shortcut for Remembering:

The reality is that when brands become misaligned, they more often push themselves into a magnetic misalignment than are being pushed by the landscape conditions around them.  It is, in fact, most often a misfortune of their own strategic misguided ways.  They lose sight of the key brand elements.  They become distracted and lose a grip on who they are and who their customers are, what they want, and how the company can provide it to them.  Yes, undoubtedly, the pull scenarios do occur. Still, in all of these instances, as demonstrated by each quadrant’s example, the hub is already naturally closer to the center of the Brand Axis.  The return to center is much easier in these situations as the company (or individual) has remained as centered as possible in the environmental and competitive pulls.  It is much faster and more likely that these companies will return to the center as soon as the landscape condition is alleviated. Still, for those misaligned push scenarios, those companies (or individuals) are voluntarily going deep into the quadrant due to internal strategic decisions.  The road to recovery is long and arduous as the center of the Brand Axis is almost at times unrecognizable, not only to you but to your target customers as well.

The Remedy to Magnetic Misalignment Is BRAND!

In conclusion, a company will never stay centered on the Brand Axis indefinitely.  There will always be decision opportunities that can and will move any company (or individual) off-center, off-brand into a misaligned state.  But the best way to prevent it as much as possible is to return to the brand elements continually.  Return to the process that established the inspiration for the brand in the first place.  If you keep the brand elements continually front and center, then we believe that not only will you stay centered in your brand messaging efforts, but over time you will start to see your message magnet grow and expand equally and dimensionally into all four quadrants of the Brand Axis.  Returning to an earlier example, we would point out a brand like Coca-Cola.  While its tagline may have changed over the years1 from “Have a Coke and a Smile” (1979), “Red, White, and You” (1986), “Life Taste’s Good” (2001), or “Open Happiness” (2009), the brand story is focused on sharing and togetherness2.  It unites people of all races, ages, economics, and tastes; it always has, and it always will.  As mentioned previously, this consistent message since 1886 has grown the message magnet on Coke’s Brand Axis to virtually cover the entire infinity loop, consistently holding the brand story as the focus of its message.  If you want your brand to become an icon, you will need to follow suit.

 

References:

  1. Coca-Cola Journey. A History of Coca-Cola Advertising Slogans.  https://www.coca-colacompany.com/stories/coke-lore-slogans
  2. We First. Coca-Cola On How Brand Story Shapes Brand Leadership.  https://www.wefirstbranding.com/brands/coca-cola-on-how-brand-story-shapes-brand-leadership/

title: 1.4 A New Inbound Model: The Social Media Magnet
html:
A New Inbound Model: The Social Media Magnet

At a holistic level, the Social Media Magnet is a theoretical and conceptual model that will guide strategic discussions throughout this courseware and methodology providing a sustainable framework. It is the process of placing a company’s message in selected media to create inertia within a defined segment.  This inertia creates energy and buzz within the targeted audience that gravitates the audience towards content that directs them into a conversion funnel whereby turning views to visitors, to leads, to consumers, to hopefully, advocates.  The Social Media Magnet is the impetus for engagement leading to goal conversions and the direct result of successful digital inbound organic marketing campaigns.  We will begin to introduce the Social Media Magnet, here and in subsequent chapters, we will detail the nuances of each element and combine the model with additional matrices to provide insight into strategic planning.

The Social Media Magnet: Using Inertia to Convert Audience to Advocates

The Social Media Magnet is our inbound model that theorizes how companies create a successful inbound marketing campaign. It has been developed and refined through years of implementation with our clients and also taught at universities The construction of our theory is made up of three parts: the brand hub, the infinity loop, and the message magnet.  The brand hub, denoted by the smaller blue circle below labeled "brand," is a culmination of the company's brand elements and is the centered balancing force of the model when properly implemented.  As you will discover, whenever the magnet becomes out of balance, it is the refocusing of the brand elements that will re-center the company and its message.  In Chapter Two, we will discuss the essential brand elements that must come first in beginning any inbound campaign.

The Social Media Magnet

The next component of the model is the infinity loop, denoted by the gray arrows assembled into a sideways figure eight (or "infinity loop" above), which represents all customers in any market segment. While consumers are positioned somewhere on this loop, they can flow in either direction concurrently, moving them towards the brand or away from the brand, most often depending on the positive or negative interpretation of a company’s message.  For this reason, the infinity loop stretches both inside and outside the message magnet’s borders (larger blue circle).  Those consumers positioned closer to the brand hub on the infinity loop are more loyal and engaged consumers while those outside of the message magnet's border are not users.  In many instances, they may not even be aware of the product, service, or content.  Additionally, the infinity loop can grow or shrink in size depending on the total size of the market segment.  However, the infinity loop does not grow or shrink at a rapid pace due to the larger cultural forces at play that makes it more difficult to grow or shrink a segment’s total market size.

Finally, there is the message magnet, denoted by the larger outer blue circle.  In the model, a company's marketing messages begin at the brand hub and flow outward to the targeted audience through communication vehicles, like a company website, social media, and email.  As these messages are delivered, they will either attract consumers toward your brand or repel them away, pushing them or pulling them along the infinity loop.  This process of attracting and repelling consumers speaks to the heart of the social magnet and the marketing message mix.  It will either keep consumers within range of hearing the marketing message, or they will move beyond the message outside of the social magnet’s impact.  In other words, consumers can potentially move beyond the borders of a company’s marketing message.  Therefore, the magnet’s borders represent the target audience to the extent that those individuals who are closer to the brand hub are more loyal and engaged consumers while those closer to the edge of the message magnet's border are only seldom or first-time users of the product, service, or content. As stated previously, those consumers outside of the border are not users at all, representing potential consumers who are either unaware or have forgotten about the company’s message due to environmental or competitive forces.  Finally, as a company reaches more consumers with its message, the size of this target audience, or message magnet, will expand and grow in diameter.  A company like Coca-Cola would have a very large message magnet, engulfing almost the entire infinity loop, because how many consumers have never heard of Coke (not many).  But a startup company may have a much smaller message magnet due to not many people in their target market having heard of them.  Hence, it's fair to say that the size of the message magnet is highly correlated with a company's market share. However, in the discussion of changing market shares, likewise, the message magnet can also shrink due to consumers moving away from the brand. The good news is, companies and organizations can carve out market segments that they can succeed in and scale.

In the following chapters, we will explore how these three parts of The Social Media Magnet, the brand hub, the infinity loop, and the message magnet should work synchronously together to provide a successful marketing campaign. When properly implemented it produces a rhythm and harmony of the message campaign that is measurable in analytics.  Although, often times the synchronization of the magnet can become misaligned.  This occurs when brand messages (coming from the brand hub) are either not what the target market finds relevant or important enough relative to other messages in the marketplace.  Sometimes these misalignments are caused by competitive forces in the market, such as a competitor coming out with a new superior product or advertisement, or they can be caused by environmental forces, such as the passing of a new law or regulation.  In fact, sometimes the misalignment can be caused merely by managerial decisions within a company that may inadvertly take the company away from its target market.  Towards the end of the courseware, we will discuss this in greater detail, but for now, we want to establish the fact that when the brand hub and the message magnet do become out of alignment, then there are negative consequences.  This event can lead to a decrease in social media traffic, website traffic, online consumer engagement, and subsequently market share, sales, and profitability.  However, through the strategies outlined in this courseware, we will instruct you on how to keep these internal components of the Social Media Magnet aligned and growing.

title: 3.2 Historical Market Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning Principles
html:
Historical Market Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning Principles

Before we address market segmentation, targeting, and positioning in a digital context, let’s first recap the historical principles that establish these marketing strategies. 

  • Market is a group of individuals or organizations that have a need for a product or service and have the ability and willingness to purchase. 
  • Target Market is a market segment.
  • Market Strategies
    • Undifferentiated targeting strategy (also known as mass marketing)
    • Concentrated targeting strategy a single marketing mix to target only one market segment.
    • Differentiated targeting strategy (also known as multi-segment targeting)
  • Marketing Myopia, which is nearsightedness when you focus more on your own needs rather than the needs of its customers. 

A market is a group of individuals or organizations that have a need for a product or service and have the ability and willingness to purchase that product or service.  Therefore, a target market is a group of individuals for which a firm has created a specific product type for a specific group of consumers.  For example, there is an entire sock market in the world.  Consumers in this market can choose from many different types of socks, including dress socks, casual socks, running socks, hiking socks, etc.  All of these different types make up the entire sock market, but consumers choosing a specific type of sock would be categorized into a market segment.

Within the entire sock market, there are many different sock manufacturers.  One firm could choose an undifferentiated targeting strategy (also known as mass marketing) and attempt to sell socks to all these different groups, or market segments, with a single marketing mix (the 5P’s of marketing).  These firms assume that all customers in this target market have similar needs, and thus the firm can satisfy most customers with little to no variation to the product.  The advantage of this approach is the potential production and marketing costs savings associated with only one style or type of product. At the same time, the disadvantages range from unimaginative product offerings to substantial competitive threats.  Most often, this targeting strategy is successful with commodities and staple food items or first movers to market.  In a historically well-defined sock market, this approach would be very difficult.

However, the sock manufacturer could also sell socks to one or more of these market segments using a concentrated targeting strategy or a differentiated target strategy.  A concentrated targeting strategy is when a firm uses a single marketing mix to target only one market segment.  The primary advantage of this strategy is that it allows a firm to specialize in a distinct consumer group.  It can concentrate its resources and specifically focus on meeting the needs of that individual market segment.  The disadvantage is that the firm runs the risk of this specialized segment being (or becoming) too small to support profitability.  Sometimes, this approach can lead to marketing myopia, which is nearsightedness when the firm's focus is more on its own needs than its customers' needs.  It prohibits seeing rapid changes in the market, and the firm operating this strategy could become quickly susceptible to changing market conditions.  This would include a manufacturer that decided to only target customers looking for running socks in the sock example.

Often, as firms deploy a successful concentrated targeting strategy, they will expand into additional market segments with a different marketing mix for each segment.  This organization strategy is known as a differentiated targeting strategy (also known as multi-segment targeting).  The advantages of this strategy most often include greater overall sales and greater financial success with economies of scale, which reduces the variable costs per unit that arise from the increased total output of a product.  However, because this strategy demands more production capacity, materials, and production labor, it most likely will result in higher overall production costs.  In continuing our sock example, a manufacturer that chooses this multi-segment strategy will target customers looking for different types of socks, providing them an option within their brand portfolio that could include running socks and hiking socks, and snow-skiing socks.  With each of these target segments, the manufacturer would highlight specific product benefits to each sock style, along with price, available retailers, and seasonal promotions for each style.

Target Market Segmentation

      1. Initially identify at least three different target segments (aka verticals) with whom your content will resonate.
      2. Determine what they need and want in content.
      3. Are there varying demographics in this group?
      4. Research to decide if these subgroups are too small/big?
      5. Determine on the right group and then name each group.
      6. Create different promotional strategies specific to each subgroup that can be replicated or serialized on a regular basis (we will discuss this more later).
      7. Review your segmentation strategy frequently to make sure that it is still resonating with the audience (use analytics).
      8. Strategically match the size of the target market with production capabilities (whether actual manufacturing or messaging frequency).
