title: 3.3 Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning in a Digital Context
html:
Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning in a Digital Context

The strategic marketing principles for inbound marketing campaigns do not change with a new digital medium, the context just changes.  Therefore, we must implement these proven principles within the parameters of this new digital medium.  To begin this process, a firm or individual should consider the different market segments to whom their digital marketing messages will appeal. 

Defining and refining your Positioning Statement

1.What is your Positioning Statement? Your positioning statement should be a concise description of your offering within your target market as well as a compelling picture of how you want that market to perceive your brand.

  • Is it simple, memorable, and tailored to the target market?
  • Does it provide an unmistakable and easily understood picture of your brand that differentiates it from your competitors?
  • Is it credible, and your brand can deliver on its promise?
  • Is your brand the sole occupier of this particular position in the market? Can you “own” it?
  • Evaluate whether or not you are making decisions that are consistent with and supportive of your brand.
  • Does it leave room for growth?

After a firm has segmented the market into viable groups and chosen a segment or segments for which to target, the firm is responsible for developing a positioning statement, giving a consumer a frame of reference for evaluating the product offering relative to other competing brands and products. The key principle of a firm’s positioning is offering superior value to its target customers. The value proposition can be derived from a single formula: Value = (Features & Benefits) / Price. The goal of the value equation is to provide superior features and benefits that are marketable for your product at a price that is competitive in the marketplace. For example, historically, Volvo cars were strongly positioned to resonate with the word “safe.” Volvo could have used all of the value propositions in its positioning statement, like image, performance, reliability, comfort. Volvo chose to double down on safety. For decades, U.S. schools and their student pickup lines were stacked front to back with Volvo’s because moms who drove them loved their kids and wanted to protect them as much as possible. Businesses and organizations like Volvo that use clearly differentiated, sustainable, and realistic positioning statements, create strong perceptions, which position them favorably in the consumer's mind relative to their competition.

Positioning statements are descriptions of your broad target market and a compelling picture of how you want your brand to be perceived by the market. It is simple, memorable, and tailored to your target market. It should provide an unmistakable and easily understood picture of your brand that differentiates it from your competitors. Also, the positioning statement should be credible and deliverable. Ensure it can truly deliver on the brand promises (Ch. 2) and that future marketing decisions can be consistent and supportive of the brand. Finally, it leaves room for growth. For a starting point, consider the following template[1].

Position Statement Template

“For [insert Target Market], the [insert Brand] is the [insert Point of Differentiation] among all [insert Frame of Reference] because [insert Reason to Believe].”

  • Target Market is the initial market segment
  • Point of Differentiation (POD) describes how your brand or product benefits customers in ways that set you apart from your competitors.
  • Frame of Reference (FOR) is the segment or category in which your company competes.
  • Reason to Believe (RTB) is just what it says. This is a statement providing compelling evidence and reasons why customers in your target market can have confidence in your differentiation claims.

Other Examples using the template “For [insert Target Market], the [insert Brand] is the [insert Point of Differentiation] among all [insert Frame of Reference] because [insert Reason to Believe].”

  • “For World Wide Web users who enjoy books, Amazon.com is a retail bookseller that provides instant access to over 1.1 million books. Unlike traditional book retailers, Amazon.com provides a combination of extraordinary convenience, low prices, and comprehensive selection.”
  • “For schools, the Underfoot Industries EverAwesome line is the strongest, most durable carpet among all commercial-grade carpets for organizations on a budget, because it is made using our patented SteelTwist technology that produces high-strength, low-wear carpets.”

Let's take a deeper look at developing the positioning statement looking at the local Nashville non-profit named Cul2vate (www.cul2vate.com). Their's looks like this: “For rehabilitative communities, Cul2vate is different from other non-profit organizations because we not only fight physical hunger but the greatest hunger of all, spiritual hunger. We engage people with food in order to create an environment where we can introduce them to their Creator.” These position statements are often turned into shorter brand statements, like Cul2vate’s: “Growing Food. Growing People.”

When considering your different target segments, be sure to consider all the types of consumers that encounter your product, service, or idea.  In this example for Cult2vate, the organization encounters various groups of people at different stages of its daily operations.  For instance, they are involved with people who love agriculture and farming, but they also interact with people who love fresh produce who do not want to work on the farm to raise it.  Additionally, they have groups of volunteers to help at the farm and they even employ ex-convicts to work on the farm.  Therefore, people who support reducing recidivism (i.e. the tendency of a convicted criminal to re-offend) can also support Cul2vate.  Finally, they sell produce to local restaurants and food-service operations, as well as donate to local food charities.

These market segments are all interested in Cul2vate and their story; nevertheless, the message targeting each of these groups will be different.  This is where the accessibility of the digital medium becomes of extraordinary benefit.  The digital messaging strategy of Cult2vate can afford to speak directly to each of these groups via their website and social media channels for little to no cost.  Unlike outbound marketing campaigns that historically would have cost Cul2vate an immense amount of money to target each of these consumers, Cul2vate can now use social media marketing to connect and deliver specialized marketing messages to each of these target market segments, which the hopes of ascertaining some goal tied to the messaging strategy, whether that would be to sign up more volunteers, promote the date of their next crop sell, or highlighting local restaurants and diners that sell their produce.  They can do all of this for no physical cost online.

Another example, Swiftwick, a Nashville-based athletic sock manufacturer has a unique product that wicks away moisture from your feet when you wear their socks (compression fit.)  Starting with just bikers, they discovered that their style of sock became especially popular with two other segments of consumers besides just bikers, but also with runners and hikers.  Before the company decided to strategically target these three market segments (also known as verticals in our text), their marketing messages targeted many different sock consumers across various sock segments.  In a desire to create some standardization and cut down on design and operating costs, Swiftwick drew its focus on these three market segments with a differentiated targeting strategy.  "Run, Bike, Hike" became their new targeted verticals to which they would focus their marketing messages. Their positioning line is designed to embrace their audiences interest and their lifestyle where they "Chase Adventure"

Like Swiftwick, firms and individuals need to understand the entire market of products or services they may offer and determine which market segment(s) they will target.  Additionally, as we have mentioned earlier in this chapter, the firm or individual needs to develop a positioning statement that speaks directly to these target markets.  In Swiftwick’s case, as you can see above, they settled on “Chase Adventure. It fits you.”  This position speaks to their thousands of consumers who are physically active and need a performance, moisture-wicking sock for their training and competitions, which allow them to chase after the thrills and adventure they seek in their outdoor activities.

The selection of these market segments (verticals) is critical in developing a successful inbound marketing campaign that will be sustainable for an extended period of time.  As one considers these market segments, the marketing strategist should consider what the group will need, want, and will connect with in the form of online content.  We will discuss this much more in the next chapter, but in considering the target segments, this content along with the channels in which they find this content should be considered.  Are these groups of consumers more likely to use Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, or Twitter?  If so, messages will need to be styled for each channel to maintain positioning continuity. What demographic variances exist in the group?  How large are the target segments and do they have any unique or specific behaviors?  All of these questions should be considered when determining the specific target segments for your product, service, or ideas.

title: 4.2 Message Harmony and Serialization
html:
Message Harmony and Serialization

There is also an important internal function of the message magnet.  Now that the individual or company has selected the primary target market or markets, the traditional marketing techniques of reach and frequency with message harmony become critically important.  Message Harmony is the process by which an individual’s or company’s narrative reinforces a consistent message across market segments.  Often these messages may be organized differently across social media channels based on character limits or presentation style. Still, the message reinforces the brand story or narrative no matter the channel or platform’s code.  When a company's narrative is repetitive and consistent across a single category of information, this process is known as Message Serialization.  These serialized groups of messages (also known as buckets) can come in the form of a narrative related to a brand, current promotions or sales, stories, news, or just fun artifacts.  For example, sneakers and athletic apparel companies have found tremendous success in driving engagement by posting recipes for athletes looking for a healthier diet.  The company or individual must identify these dimensionally repetitive groups of messages that will be communicated across its various target markets (verticals).  The target segments by serialized message interaction (vertical x bucket interaction) will become a key strategic process for keeping your message magnet centered and productive as we move forward with the other components of our digital inbound strategy, like goal funnel conversions.

Next, within the message magnet, as consumers become aware and engage with the individual or company, they are immediately placed within a goal funnel housed within the hub of the social media magnet (i.e., at the website or blog), which uses marketing analytics to measure each level of the conversion process.  Again, depending on the goal of the conversion process, whether it is to increase likes, followers, sales, etc., various goal funnel processes can be implemented at each stage of the conversion process.  Future chapters will discuss this process and the strategies needed to convert at higher rates, but for now, it is important to conceptually understand how the Social Media Magnet works to attract and engage consumers, pulling them into the goal funnel process. First, it uses the spokes (social media channels) to attract these consumers to interesting content.  Then, through hyperlinks, it directs consumers into the hub (website) to engage them in a call-to-action process, which initiates the goal funnel tracking process.  The company or individual blogger can then rely on marketing analytics to help track the goal conversion process to monitor the audience's progress.  If the goals are being met, then the process is working.  However, if the goals are not being met, the auditing process will demonstrate where the individual or company may need to tweak the process to drive a higher conversion rate of the desired goal. Therefore, a consistent monitoring process is always encouraged as an internal audit program.

Finally, we want to reiterate the possibility that both the message magnet and infinity loop can expand and contract based on the efforts of the individual or company running the social media marketing campaign.  As alluded to previously, both the message magnet and the infinity loop for Coca-Cola are theoretically enormous.  Is there anyone in the world who hasn’t heard of Coca-Cola or considered purchasing the product?  Hence, the potential size of the defined market that is their consideration set would almost envelop the entire target audience represented by the infinity loop.  However, if you were a startup company in the motorcycle business, naturally, your infinity loop will be smaller than Coke’s.  This is because there are not as many people who drive motorcycles as people who drink Coca-Cola.  Likewise, that startup motorcycle company’s message magnet will be much smaller compared to an established competitor, like Harley Davidson, on the same size infinity loop.  But over time, a successful social media marketing campaign could make the size of that message magnet grow larger and larger as brand awareness, sales, and market share increase.  As both the message magnet and infinity loop expand and contract, different social media strategies need to be deployed, which we will also discuss in subsequent chapters.

title: 4.3 The Message Matrix: Turning Marketing Principles into Inbound Strategy

The Message Matrix: Turning Marketing Principles into Inbound Strategy

As we have indicated previously in this text and will continue to reinforce, the strategic marketing principles for inbound marketing campaigns do not change just because the medium has changed.  The historical principles of marketing still apply in a digital environment, and it is the context that changes.  We still use the proven marketing principles but now within a new medium; therefore, we must implement them within the parameters of this digital medium.  In Chapter 2, an ample amount of text was devoted to developing key brand elements for a firm or organization.  In building the brand elements of story, promises, beliefs, and trust, a brand narrative was created that will serve as the balancing force for keeping future messages centered and “on brand” in the digital environment.  In Chapter 3, the next process determined to whom and how those online digital messages will be delivered.  We still have to discover the market segments, choose one or more target segments, and deliver a positioning statement that resonates with customers and differentiates our firm from the competition. 

In this chapter, the third step has been to determine the common group of messages (or buckets) to serialize content over an extended period.  The Message Matrix is a strategic planning tool that will combine the chosen target market segments (verticals) with the serialized messages (buckets) to create a strategic matrix for who the company or individual will target and what they will say on a rolling editorial basis.

These cells of interaction between the targeted group and the targeted message (aka as the vertical x bucket interaction) will serve as a focused, dedicated message that you can serialize across their media channels on a continual basis as part of a rolling calendar of editorial content.  We will discuss this calendar more in the next chapter, but for now, the matrix below gives you a great visual of what the message matrix should strategically look like when formulated correctly. In addition, your level assignments will allow you to create a message matrix of your own for your coming live campaign.

This section of your Message Matrix creates the paths for your sterilized message Buckets are your Serialized Topics, and Verticals are your Target Audience segments you previously identified. This approach creates lanes and paths for the ongoing creation of your messaging campaigns and avoids the pitfalls of not knowing what to say or straying off the message. As we move forward and build this out, you will see how it will eventually populate into the ongoing promotional calendar.

.

Think of these as intersections of your messaging that both touch the topics you have identified and are relevant to your audience. To highlight this process, we will continue to use non-profit Cul2vate from the previous chapter. 

In Chapter 3, the potential target markets for Cul2vate were identified. They included groups of individuals interested in these topics: agriculture, reducing recidivism, individuals purchasing produce, and restaurants that use organic produce as ingredients.  In short, we will label these four groups as agriculture, recidivism, purchasing, and restaurants.  These targeted groups of consumers (verticals) will be put across the top of each column of our matrix. Then, along the side of the matrix, for each row, we will include the serialized group of messages (buckets) that will focus on content that will be delivered to each of the targeted groups of individuals.  This serialized content for Cul2vate revolves around messages that they want to communicate to their target audiences, like information about the produce they grow, messages about their cul2vators (ex-convicts working on the farm), special notes about their training curriculum, identifying their strategic partners, and messages to and for recruiting new volunteers.

title: 5.3 Retention Post-Follower Email Campaigns
html:
Retention Post-Follower Email Campaigns

When the content strategy is working, the target audience will be funneled through the goal conversion process, and in many instances, will become a follower of your content.  At this time, one primary goal conversion that should be capitalized upon is ascertaining the target audience’s email.  In fact, email is the absolute hardest bit of personal data that you can collect from your followers. From the authors’ experiences, consumers are more likely to give you credit card information than their personal email addresses.  Therefore, when you can and do ascertain this information, you must protect and nurture a relationship through the email built on trust and respect.  Remember your brand promises, and make absolutely sure to uphold them as you create your email campaign.

A direct email campaign should be strategically designed to optimize deliverability and convert email sign-up campaigns to reach regular lists of email recipients while developing engagement and relationships.  Customer acquisition should be based on "relationship," not marketing; therefore, the social media magnet email campaign should be designed as a warm, friendly, personal email from the sender to the recipient.  To ensure these goals, the email campaign should be designed around the 2+2+2 email rule.  This rule functions to ensure timeliness (instead of a Marketing email which can easily be set aside for later), avoid redundancy by minimizing the effect of a repetitive header image, and increase readability by appearing conversational in nature. First, let's discuss your email will look.

Sending images in emails create lots of problems. They often arrive as broken image links, so the recipient does not even see them, or they are attached to the email as a separate item. In addition, header images are redundant, making each new email look just like the previous and pushing the content further down the page. These are some of the main reasons emails will be ignored or not read till later because they look like "marketing," not communication that is of value to the recipient.

Instead, The Social Media Magnet email strategy is designed around a text-based version, even though it is in HTML format with clickable links, to make it look readable and friendly. These types of emails with no context images eliminate the need for a required download, making them immediately readable, mobile-friendly, and "light."  The principal focus of the email is on content and the click-through to the website for conversion opportunities.

Now let's look at the 2+2+2 email rule.

The 2+2+2 email strategy operates under the same guidelines as an email from one person to another (person-to-person), being that it has no logo attached or marketing header.  Graphic images and traditional marketing emails require digital pictures to be downloaded.  This produces a strong resistance to read through the email and can also cause broken images, and in some cases, virtually unreadable email.  Additionally, graphically formatted marketing emails are associated with solicitation or even "hard sell" ad emails. Finally, graphical header displays push the content below the fold.  Images and branding beyond email content need to be built into the on-page content and design of the website and may need to include a vertical landing page strategy.

The 2+2+2 Email Rule: Improving Opens, reducing Opt-outs, and Increasing Click Rate.

  • 2 seconds to see who it is from - Someone in the Company and Company Name
  • 2 seconds to see what it is about - The Subject Line
  • 2 seconds to check the body of the email to get the content, determine interest, and click to continue to the site for more.

Here, emails are always sent from an “individual/name” email address of the person who is consistently monitoring the account, not sent from a “role address” like “webmaster” or “info.”  In fact, most spam filters and email services are becoming more and more stringent, blocking role addresses from even delivering into their systems.  Likewise, emails are never sent from a “No Reply” email address because it is bad form to send someone an email and then tell them they cannot reply to that email.  In this case, the email monitor is responsible for responding to or forwarding a reply email to the proper person for response.  Additionally, using a consistent monitor also reduces the difficulty of email delivery when the sending email address is frequently changing. Finally, a qualified email service delivery provider (e.g., Constant Contact, MailChimp) should be utilized to maintain maximum deliverability, ensuring whitelist compliance (the ability of the individual to unsubscribe from the list in one to two clicks) of the sending URL and the ability of the recipient to manage their individual email preferences, including list opt-out.

The Social Media Magnet textbase emails have proven superior open rates and click-through rates well above industry averages, sometimes double the rates with negligible opt-outs and little to no spam reports.

Content focusing on emails should always be monitored, tracked, and improved to ensure campaign success. Still, previous use of this email strategy has supplied over 1 million emails a month with superior results.  This strategic approach to email campaigns is designed around an email personality, not the company or role addresses.  This email campaign approach using the 2+2+2 email rule will provide superior results for any individual or company willing to utilize these strategies.

title: 6.3 Designing the Editorial Calendar:  Planning Content
html:
Designing the Editorial Calendar: Planning Content

Over the last few chapters, we have been working through the Message Matrix, pressing towards planning a calendar in the last section, showing the metamorphosis of transferring strategic ideas related to market segmentation, targeting, and positioning into the tactical process of creating a rolling editorial calendar.  It began with identifying vertical segments and serialized buckets of messages, identifying the correct social media channels for those target markets, and thinking about the interaction of all three components. 

Content Planning, Scheduling & Distribution

    1. Blogs & Search Engines:  Writers should be working closely within Search Engine Optimization (SEO) strategies to determine what keywords are most important -- ideally a combination of long-tail terms and head terms, at an appropriate level of competitiveness given your domain authority and how aggressively you can go after the terms. Of course, that content should also be optimized for on-page SEO to improve its chances of ranking highly. 
    2. Social Media:  The content you create should be shared on the social networks on which you're active. Moreover, Google's algorithm considers social signals as one of its most important ranking factors -- socially shared content is a vote of approval, or at the very least important, so it makes sense Google would consider it when deciding whether a post should rank well in organic search.
    3. Email:  Email lists are marketer's most treasured assets -- and they're a smart way to drive traffic, conversions, and re-conversions on your content. Invest in growing your blog email subscription list for an incredibly valuable distribution arm alongside your sales lists.
    4. Social Ads & PPC:  Digital advertising isn't inherently bad. In fact, targeted spend can help certain pieces of content get unprecedented amplification when you find an efficient CPC if it seems like this feeds into the initial problem that drove you to content marketing in the first place.

Now, we need to put that into an editorial calendar that is easy to follow and provides a nice visualization of the planned content.  Let's look at a 90-day rolling calendar example for Cul2vate below.  We will examine three (3) different 30-day sections (first 30 days, second 30 days, and last 30 days) to identify what content they have planned and is scheduled (highlighted in yellow) versus what content they have planned and still need to create/curate (highlighted in green) versus what content that has not planned yet (highlighted in white).  Let's look at the first thirty days.

 

 

As we can see from the calendar above, Cul2vate has its first 30 days of content from this date rolling forward completed, planned, and scheduled on their social media management tool (CoSchedule).  They will highlight in their blog a recent cult2vator graduate named Ricky, who has finished his year-long program with Cul2vate, staying out of jail and supporting himself while working on the farm.  They also plan to blog some fun news regarding the week of work on the farm.  They have their Facebook focus planned for every day (choosing not to post on Sunday due to their religious mission) and have three features they want to highlight on Tuesday, which are directed on continuing the process of creating relationships with their newsletter subscribers.  Remember, the email has a retention focus, while the social media channels have an acquisition focus.  Currently, Cul2vate is primarily focused on just one social media channel, Facebook.  If they were to expand into other social channels, they could extend this calendar by adding more rows just above the National Month Reminder to include other social channels, like Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter, etc.  Finally, notice that they don't post a blog in every serialized bucket category (blog focus rows) every week.  They mix up these messages across weeks to give a good balance of new, fresh content every week.  Let's look at the next 30-days of the rolling calendar, which is the 60-day planning outlook.

 

 

Here we see that Cul2vate does not have all of the content planned or scheduled.  The first week of August is all planned, but they still have two pieces of content (highlighted in green) to write and schedule within CoSchedule.  As you get later into this month of content, you see that more pieces need to be scheduled (in green) and even planned (blank spaces in white).  In these instances, the social media coordinator needs to be speaking with people within the company to see if there are any ideas on what to plan and to ask if anyone would be willing to write a blog or post for these spaces that need to be filled.  Also, notice the weekly focus at the top of the excel planner.  Each week provides a general weekly theme to build consistency in the message.  Tying these weekly focuses back into the brand story is a great way to continue to strengthen the brand narrative and promises, which will, in turn, build brand belief and trust. Finally, let's take a look at the 90-day planning outlook.

 

 

This 90-day outlook is typical for the process.  As we can see, an effort is still going into finishing out the 60-day outlook, so planning for the 90-day is just beginning.  Cul2vate needs to determine their weekly focus for each week and then start planning for each blog, Facebook post, and weekly email newsletter.  It also needs to search for any special holidays or national month ideas in September for which they could creatively use in their planning, like Labor Day in Week 1.

Content distribution is all about making sure the content you create gets found by the widest audience possible. This is the step a lot of content marketing teams skip, and here are a couple of ideas of why:

Mistake #1: The mere act of publishing content regularly does a lot of the "distribution" work for you -- if you consider search engines a distribution channel. (Which we do, considering how often people use them to find content.) If you create content regularly informed by keyword research and optimized for search, Google takes care of the rest of your content distribution plan.

Mistake #2: Many content marketing teams are made up of writers rather than marketers. In my experience, writers are less interested in marketing their content and more interested in just writing cool stuff. The same goes for designers -- often, they would rather spend time creating something beautiful than functional and marketing it.

Excuses aside, if a content marketing team stops short of content distribution, they're only doing half their job. It's content marketing, after all. So let's explore the most valuable channels you have at your disposal for distributing your content.

The finalized editorial calendar for each company or individual will vary based on the number of target segments, buckets of serialized messages, social media channels incorporated into the message matrix, and how many resources are available to the company or firm.  But most importantly, each company or individual must have a rolling editorial calendar.  The entire inbound marketing campaign premise is built on having this calendar, and it is working for you to plan and schedule creative content with messages on-brand.  We will get to what happens when messages are off-brand in the last three chapters of this text, but now, right now, it's not pretty.  A misaligned magnet can have dire consequences on the success of your inbound marketing campaign.  However, staying up-to-date with your editorial calendar should help minimize these misalignments and keep you in a successful lane of targeted messages and digital growth.

title: 8.4 WordPress Blog Creation: Steps to Optimize Performance
html:
WordPress Blog Creation: Steps to Optimize Performance

This section will help with the actual WordPress blogs that you will “post” to your website.

Upon clicking to add a new post to the blog page, be sure to wait until the very end of this process to enter the post's title.  Once you add the title, a permalink will be created related to the blog title.  Once this is entered, if you go back and change the title after writing the blog, the permalink will not change.  You would have to change the permalink BEFORE you schedule this post manually.  Many forget to do this, and therefore, the permalink does not match the blog title.  So again, WAIT on the blog title.

Next, be sure to immediately change the date for when this blog post will publish.  WordPress always starts with “Publish Immediately” in the right-hand sidebar.  Because you plan these posts weeks in advance using the message matrix and the rolling editorial calendar, you will NEVER be publishing these blogs immediately. 

Schedule when to Publish

  • WordPress Default is “Publish Immediately” in the right-hand sidebar.
  • Always Schedule – this allows you to plan ahead
  • Avoid Broken Links
    • Always confirm Post is Published BEFORE sharing to Social or email
    • You will see it if logged in, but it will not be publicly available.
    • NEVER Post a Preview Link; check your URL before posting to social

You will ALWAYS be scheduling them.  Therefore, you need to click the “Edit” button next to publish immediately to schedule the upcoming date and time for when this blog will post to your website.  Once this date and time are sent, the blue “Publish” button will change to a blue “Schedule” button.  This will be the button you click at the end of this process to complete your blog post.

Creating a Blog Post

  • Once you add the title, a permalink will be created related to the blog title. 
  • If you change the title/subject - manually change the permalink BEFORE you schedule this post.
  • This will help with your SEO

Moving forward, before you begin writing any copy, you need to choose the picture that will be associated with this blog.  You have an idea of the content already since you planned this weeks ago, which means you have an idea of what picture you want to be associated with this blog.  So, first, click on the “Add Media” button at the top of the center menu options, just underneath where the blog title will be entered.  With this button, you will upload and place the featured image you want to be associated with this blog.  This image is vital as it will be the image connected to your social media posts, placed within your website blog list, etc.  Once you have placed this picture within the text box, where you will write your copy, then you need to set the image as the official image for this blog.  This is done by scrolling to the very bottom of the right-hand sidebar. 

Featured Image

  • Always put an image with the proper name/title on the image file
  • Search engines will rank and score your image as well as your content
  • “Set Featured Image.” so you have a consistent presentation of your articles, especially in archives and categories.

There will be an option called “Set Featured Image.”  Click on this link and follow the instruction for setting your image as the featured image.  When complete, that image will also be displayed in the sidebar in the “Featured Image” section to confirm that this will be the featured image for this blog post.  Note, you should only set ONE featured image in the blog, even if you use multiple pictures within the body of the blog.  The first image on the page should always be the only featured image.

 

Additionally, within the text box, write the blog copy.  If you cite an outside source within the blog, do NOT use the hyperlink tool for these citations within the blog copy. Instead, use a number to refer to the exact citation in the references at the bottom of the blog.  Place the hyperlink within the reference citation at the end of the blog.  Any hyperlinks that will take a reader away from your blog should NOT be included in the body of the blog.  You want them to read all the way through your content before they click a link that would take them off-site to curated content.  However, if you are using a call-to-action from your own website as a registration form, add that hyperlink within the blog copy but at the end of the blog.  Again, you want them to read all of the content before clicking away.

Now that the blog has been fully created, the next step is to identify the categories and tags associated with the blog.  The blog category should coincide with which “Bucket” your blog is classified.  Again, refer back to Chapter 4 in the discussion of message serialization. 

Categories and Tags

  • Limit Categories and Tags to relevancy
  • Do NOT duplicate your Categories and Tag; it is redundant
  • Do not add Post/Articles to more than one category; it looks bad and is Redundant
  • Do not use the same Tags on all Post/Articles

These groups of serialized messages were classified as buckets.  In reality, you should only have 5-6 blog categories that exactly match your message matrix buckets.  For example, Cul2vate had five buckets, including Produce, Cul2vators, Training Curriculum, Partners, and Volunteers.  In this case, if the blog were about growing techniques for the farm, then the correct category here would be Produce.  Once you have selected the appropriate bucket as your category, you should identify the tags associated with this blog.  Again, think of tags, like hashtags for Twitter.  WordPress tags search terms that will allow a reader to search all blogs in your created blogosphere that have to do with the associated tags.  In other words, if I tag “Knee” for every blog related to knee pain for a physical therapy website, then readers who have a knee issue can click on the “Knee” tag and see all of the blogs the PT clinic has ever written about knee pain.  Tags are just useful search terms that will be important to your future readers.

Add Citations and Credits

  • Do not plagiarize; it’s a no-no
  • Careful about linking off your site
    • External Links – Open link in New Window to keep them on your site
    • Internal Links – open in the same window to navigate your site

Finally, once your blog has been completed with the identified featured image and referenced sources, now go back and title the blog correctly.  Once you have named the blog and have the correct identifying permalink mutually created, you can click the blue “Schedule” button to complete the blog creation process.

Check your work after Publishing

  • Be sure to Preview your Post/Article to see what it looks like
  • After it publishes, check it out and make sure it is as you planned.
  • Check how your Content looks in Category. Archive and Tag groupings to ensure it looks as planned.

title: 9.4 Social Formatting: Steps to Optimize Your Social Referrals to the Hub
html:
Social Formatting: Steps to Optimize Your Social Referrals to the Hub

Like the previous chapter, this last section will help create social media posts to assist in bringing traffic back to your website.  Let’s begin with the demographic content reported by the Pew Research Center1 from the last section.  Here it is again, but with some additional variables:

Based on previous practicum exercises, you have already defined multiple target markets, so you should already be aware of these demographics.  However, if you did not use this type of research to select your preferred social media channels, this would be a good time to revisit your previous selections.  Depending on the demographics of your target audience, you are most likely going to choose your primary channels from the list above.  Most importantly, you should first consider the overall total of people who use these channels.  As we have already discussed, Facebook and YouTube more than double the next closest channel, Instagram, in overall total use.  Therefore, we would suggest you at least have one, if not both of these, somewhere in your strategic content plan.  If video production is not within your skillset, then Facebook is the obvious choice, even though videos are getting significant bumps in the reach algorithm right now on the Facebook platform.  Additional variables to consider are gender, ethnicity, income, education, and geographic location.  You might be surprised by research that indicates the value of certain niches on each channel, e.g., Hispanic women on Twitter.

Next, be sure to know the picture size requirements for each of your social media channels.  Every channel requires a different size.  For example, picture requirements for Facebook are a little larger than for LinkedIn.  The picture that looks appropriate for one channel may not look appropriate for another.  As demonstrated below, the full Facebook photo provides a good reference to balance.  Unfortunately, the same photo posted to LinkedIn loses all connotations because the photo size requirements are different.  Be sure to have a working knowledge of all of your channel requirements and account for each of those as you schedule your posts.

As you schedule your posts for social media, a general rule is to check your mobile visualization first.  Mobile applications display fewer characters than tablets or desktops before collapsing your posts into a “see more” screen utilization function.  This occurs for obvious reasons because the screen size is smaller.  However, users are less likely to click through to your website when the hyperlink is buried behind this functionality.  Since post etiquette requires the content creator to put the hyperlink at the end of the post, if the interface hides the link, many users will not click on the “see more” link to open the rest of the post and then click on your link.  Therefore, we recommend only 2-3 short sentences for each social media post, especially if you have a hyperlink driving the traffic back to your website.  Under all circumstances, you want that link to be visible.  Therefore, this is why we recommend designing the post with mobile in mind.  If the link is visible in mobile, it will be visible in tablet and desktop form.  Additionally, mobile Internet usage worldwide surpassed that of desktop usage at the end of 20162, and as of 2018, worldwide internet usage was 52.2% mobile, up from 50.3% the previous year3.

Remember, not every post on your social media spokes has to be a call-to-action or a hyperlink driving traffic back to the website.  Sometimes, especially at the beginning of the brand campaign, you need to build the brand.  You need to have some posts that don’t require anyone but entertain or highlight something interesting about the brand or its story.  Jokes, curated stories, feel-good songs, or inspirational quotes are important when creating brand awareness.  Some strategies even use a “National Day of...” to promote something original or unexpected.  Maybe for National Aunt Day, you highlight someone close to the brand who wants to thank their aunt for a special reason or just being a great aunt.  Those emotional connections to your audience are important.  They demonstrate that it’s not all business all the time, but that there is someone human sitting behind the computer screen on the other end of the Internet.  We are human (except for Wikipedia and other bots), and it’s good to remind people of that sometimes.  A human touch goes a long way in brand building.

 

References:

1. Pew Research Center: Social Media Use in 2018. http://www.pewinternet.org/2018/03/01/social-media-use-in-2018/

2. TechCrunch: Mobile Internet Use Passes Desktop for the First Time, Study Finds.  https://techcrunch.com/2016/11/01/mobile-internet-use-passes-desktop-for-the-first-time-study-finds/

3. BlueCorona.com: 61 Mobile Marketing Statistics for 2018 and Beyond.  https://www.bluecorona.com/blog/mobile-marketing-statistics

11.2 SEO Tools & Setting Up Yoast SEO on WordPress

Now that you know what SEO is and that it will never die off, it is time to set it up on your website and figure out how it works. 

By now, you should have identified the general terms that you associate with your brand. The next step is to break this down into the Keywords you will focus on and then implement them on your website to maximize your search and engagement. You will need to make sure you cover all the bases to optimize your content and pages properly.

How to Implement Keywords on Your Website

    1. Page Titles/Blog Titles
    2. Content Tags (not categories)
    3. Content on Page
    4. Permalink URL Structure::  https://socialmediamagnetpro.com/blog/articles/drive-your-brand-with-strategic-messaging-video/
    5. Meta descriptions (with Yoast SEO)
    6. File names of images on a page - Yes, name your images properly! Search engines look for image titles and names as well as the image itself.

Aggregate all of this together to maximize your position in search results.

The best way to do this in WordPress is to set up an SEO plugin.  There are several good ones, like All in One SEO and Yoast SEO.  We will use the latter; therefore, the following is a step-by-step guide on how to set up Yoast SEO on your website.

First, from your WordPress Dashboard, you need to go to your plugins menu and select “Add Plugins.”  In the menu bar near the top of the screen, type in “Yoast SEO,” where it says “Search Plugins...”  You need to install the Yoast SEO plugin that looks like this:

Once this plugin has been installed and activated, you need to click on the Yoast SEO menu in the left-hand sidebar of your WordPress dashboard.  On the General page, you should see a configuration wizard like below.  You need to click on the configuration wizard setup link for the first-time setup of Yoast.

Once you click on the configuration link shown above, then follow these steps to set up your Yoast SEO plugin:

1. Click on the options window below to start the configuration wizard.

2. Set the environment option to either live or under construction, depending on the status of your campaign.  If it has already started, then click live.  If you are still building in preparation for the campaign kickoff, then choose the under construction option, as seen below.

3. Set the Site-type.  Choose what type of site you will be running on the website. This will help optimize your site for all search engines.

4. Set the site description for either a person or company.  Enter your individual name or company name with the brand logo.

5. Input your social profiles that you will be using for the campaign into the social profiles form.

6. Specify which post types you want search engines to index.  We recommend that both posts and pages are allowed to be indexed.

7. Specify if you will have multiple authors or not.  In this class, you will check: No.

8. Skip the Google Search Console.  Do not Authenticate.  Google Search Console is a tool from Google that allows you to view information about how your site works in Google's organic search.  While Google Search Console is definitely something you should investigate eventually, it’s not necessary to maintain Yoast SEO right now or for this project.

9. Insert your website name and the title separator you want to use.  We always recommend the dash, which has been pre-selected for you.

10. Newsletter: It’s your choice of whether or not you want to sign up for the Yoast Newsletter.  They do provide some valuable information relative to news and tips in the world of SEO.  It is up to you.

11. Instructional Videos:  You can watch these videos at your leisure for deeper insight into training and upgrading to Yoast Premium.  Premium is not needed for this class project.

12. Success: Congratulations, you have successfully set up Yoast SEO for your website to optimize your search results for your project.

13. Check for any Yoast SEO Problems.  After you have closed the Yoast SEO Configuration Wizard, be sure to check your Yoast SEO General settings page for any problems that may have occurred during installation.  A frequent error message is presented below.

If you get the “blocking access” error message (seen above), you will need to check your Search Engine Visibility by clicking on the Settings: Reading Tab in your WordPress dashboard.  Be sure that the “Discourage search engines from indexing this site” is UNCHECKED.  If it is checked, then search engines will not crawl your site.  Having this check-in place is good as you construct the site and don’t want uninvited visitors.  But once you launch the website, you need to uncheck this box to allow search engines to do their magic.  Note:  If you had checked Environment Option B (Under construction) in Step 2 of this section, then this option would have been checked to prevent search engines from crawling your site until you were ready to launch.

If there are no Yoast SEO problems, then your website’s search engine results are configured and ready to be optimized.  In the next section, we will teach you how to use your Yoast SEO plugin, how to interact with it, and how to analyze its results.

Setting up Meta Description Templates by Content-Type

As stated back in the first section of this chapter, on a day-to-day basis, the metadata is where you and website visitors will interact with search engine results the most.  The metadata is what the viewer will read just under the title and URL of their search engine results.  For example, if you were to Google search for “Yoast SEO,” then one of the first-page results will appear like this:

The metadata explains to the person searching Yoast SEO that “Yoast helps with your website optimization, whether it be through our widely used SEO software or our online SEO courses: we’re here to help.”  Writing your own meta-description allows you to optimize your SEO content for quality and readability.  To find and edit the meta-description content types in Yoast SEO, go to the Yoast SEO: Search Appearance tab in the left-hand sidebar of the WordPress dashboard. Then click on “Content Types” in the overhead tabs, as seen below.

As seen above, scrolling down in the “Content Types” tab will lead you to the Meta-description box for BOTH posts and pages.  Here is where you can set up the overall template for your posts and page meta descriptions.  We recommend leaving these templates as they are for now while you are learning SEO.  However, with more experience in the future, you may want to come back to this location to set up a template that is more conducive to your exact post or page meta descriptions.

Changing Actual Post or Page Meta Descriptions During Content Creation

When you are creating (or editing) either a blog post or a page on your website, the Yoast SEO plugin provides options for you on the WordPress creation page for editing your meta-descriptions.  After you have written your blog or finished building your webpage, then you can work on your search engine optimization for this blog or page.  This is controlled through the on-page Yoast SEO Meta Box.  This box is located just below where you would enter the text for either your blog post or page on your website.  Both are displayed below.

As seen above, in the red annotated box, you can enter the description that you want everyone to see when they search for content on this post (or page).  Be sure to keep it concise.  After you have finished, Google your post (or page) title to confirm that the correct meta-description is used.  If it is too long and you notice that the description within Google moves into a “See more...” function on-page, then go back and shorten your meta-description.  Like in previous chapters, we want the entire description visible, specifically for search engine users.

Next, you will want to enter some important keywords for this post or page.  These focal keywords can be added in the blue annotated box in the Yoast SEO box picture above (from the previous paragraph).  As we described in the first section of this chapter, you can use Google Adwords Keyword Planner to search the use of specific keywords.  For example, if I wanted to add a keyword that revolved around either digital marketing or social media to my blog post, then a keyword planner search would return results that look like this:

Historical context: this section describes Facebook changes in 2016–2018. Its screenshots and menu references document that period. Use the Pro Analytics application below and the current channel interfaces for today’s workflow.

12.2 Facebook User Displeasure Actually Leads to Less, but Better Organic Content

At this stage, according to Social Flow, organic reach was still dropping at a rate of 42% between January and May of 20161.  Ironically, however, Facebook users noticed the trend of more and more ad content in their timeline news feeds, along with a plethora of uninteresting, low-quality organic posts.  Through both, Facebook users began voicing their displeasure as posts from businesses, brands, and media were crowding out the personal moments that led users to connect more with each other in the first place2.  Facebook realized they had to fix this saturation issue by changing the algorithm.  They needed to promote high-quality, personalized content to continue building meaningful relationships in the social space.

In the blog post announcing the algorithm change, Facebook Engineering Director Lars Backstrom indicated the new algorithm update would try to ensure that “stories posted directly by friends that you care about, such as photos, videos, status updates or links, will be higher up in the News Feed, so you are less likely to miss them.”  He also warned that Pages could anticipate a dip in organic reach and referral traffic for some pages and encouraged Pages to post things they know their audiences are likely to share with their friends3.  With this change, Social Flow adjusted their original report from 42% to a decrease of 52% from January to July of 20164.

Furthermore, Facebook doubled down on this commitment to friends and family in the next two years.  In 2017, Facebook did not change the algorithm but rather changed the News Feed function entirely.  In October, Facebook tested an ad-free News Feed that users could switch to, dedicated to publisher content rather than personal content. To businesses, it clearly foreshadowed a Facebook that separated business/brand content from friends/family content.  Today, that "alternative News Feed" is known as the "Pages" option on the left-hand sidebar of a user's News Feed5.

In 2018, Facebook again updated its News Feed algorithm.  This update did not eliminate Page content entirely but set different priorities on what would be posted to users’ News Feed.  Paul Armstrong provides a great article about a Facebook webinar that shared these priorities at Forbes.com6.  He highlights what Facebook prioritizes as important for News Feeds:

  • People sharing a link over Messenger
  • Commenting on or liking a person's photo or status updates
  • Multiple replies to a status update or photo = more likely to see again
  • Meaningful interactions - this doesn't mean 'like if you agree.'

He also notes that Facebook wants content publishers to have other people share their content with Facebook and not be the initial publisher of the content.  That means content creation on blog sites needs to have social posts buttons that allow users to post into space rather than posting it directly into the social space.  Facebook also provided additional tips for content publishers from this webinar.

Additional Tips for Content Publishers:

  • Have other people share your content on Facebook.
  • Start getting journalists to comment and spur on activity.
  • Focus on content that other people will share.
  • Create stories that can be updated.
  • Use paid media to create spikes on relevant content.
  • Start thinking about local products.
  • Start pushing the 'Follow' function for Pages.
  • Stop tagging.
  • Become engaged in Facebook Groups.

Finally, shares and comments, in particular, are considered "active" interactions, which Facebook considers more "meaningful" when slotting content on a user's News Feed. For that reason, video watch time, referral traffic, and organic reach might even decrease this year if the content does not create a meaningful interaction7.
